headline: High risk of prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared web/MCP workflows; compliance exposure is also material.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A ingests web content, files, MCP, and OpenAPI tool outputs; Agent B uses MCP and function-calling against plugins. That creates a direct path for attacker-controlled content from A into B’s instruction-following context, especially if A’s outputs are reused as plugin inputs. No provenance or isolation is documented, so uncertainty pushes severity up.
conditions: IF Agent A forwards web or file content into Agent B prompts without provenance tags, injection is reachable.
IF a shared MCP server or plugin returns untrusted text that B treats as instructions, hijack risk materializes.
mitigations: Disable automatic prompt chaining between A and B.
Add provenance labels to all A outputs before B consumes them.
Restrict B to allowlisted plugins only.
Insert a manual review step for any web-sourced text.
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization and instruction/data separation in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches prompts, chat messages, documents, files, notes, calendar events, persistent memory, and API keys, while Agent B reads and writes filesystem data and sends requests to external model providers. If they share a workspace or memory store, sensitive data from A can flow into B and then out over B’s broad network egress. The pair’s default surfaces make leakage plausible.
conditions: IF A and B share a mounted directory or memory store, A’s documents or API keys can be read by B.
IF B forwards its context to external model APIs, any imported sensitive data can leave the boundary.
mitigations: Separate A and B into distinct workspaces.
Remove secrets from any shared directory.
Turn off B access to sensitive folders.
Use per-agent credentials and storage.
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before B sends context to external APIs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can write local files and mounted volumes and spawn subprocesses; B can read and write the filesystem, use MCP, and operate with shared state via a memory store. Their write surfaces overlap on mutable resources, so concurrent edits or state corruption are plausible even though B cannot modify git state or execute shell. The overlap is real but not maximally destructive.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or memory store, last-writer-wins corruption can occur.
IF A writes artifacts while B rewrites them concurrently, file races are possible.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Make shared artifacts read-only for one agent.
Use per-agent namespaces in the memory store.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks on shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can browse, call tools, and generate artifacts; B is an orchestration layer that can consume application context and invoke plugins. If B treats A’s outputs as authoritative, errors or hallucinations from A can cascade into downstream actions or external API calls. No verification gate is documented, so the pair is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated text as plugin input without validation, incorrect actions can propagate.
IF A produces fabricated facts that B renders or acts on, downstream harm can occur.
mitigations: Require citation checks before B acts on A outputs.
Add a human approval step for external side effects.
Limit B to read-only summarization of A outputs.
Log and diff A outputs before reuse.
requires-engineering: implement schema validation for A-to-B handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: A explicitly handles calendar events, usage analytics, model evaluation data, files, and API keys; B handles model provider API keys and plugin credentials. Both can send data to external model providers and cloud services, but the profiles do not document residency or certification mismatches. The compliance risk is therefore a likely policy-gap issue rather than a proven breach.
conditions: IF EU personal data is routed through either agent without a DPA, residency/compliance issues arise.
IF PHI or regulated secrets are placed into A or B, their documented cloud/API paths may violate policy.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent.
Block regulated data from external APIs.
Review vendor DPAs and retention settings.
Store secrets only in approved vaults.
requires-engineering: enforce residency-aware routing and audit logging.
